entries.term: a / an for first mention, the for second: I saw a dog. The dog …
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Use *a/an* when you first mention a singular countable thing the listener doesn't know yet, and *the* when you mention it again, because now the listener knows which one.
entries.usage: This is the basic system of English articles, in every register. Plurals and uncountables have no article or *some* at first mention (*some apples … the apples*). Something connected to the first noun can also take *the* right away (*a bakery … the owner*).
entries.pattern: a / an + noun (new to the listener) → the + noun (already known)
examples: **A man** and **a woman** walked into the café, and **the woman** ordered for both of them.
I ordered **a salad** and **a burger**. **The salad** was great, but **the burger** was cold.
There's **a new bakery** on Elm Street. **The owner** used to work in Paris.

drill.sentence: I saw a fox in the yard this morning. {{The}} fox was eating our tomatoes.
drill.hint: Choose a or the: I saw a fox in the yard this morning. ___ fox was eating our tomatoes.

mistake.wrong: I bought new jacket yesterday. A jacket is really warm.
mistake.right: I bought a new jacket yesterday. The jacket is really warm.
mistake.why: A singular countable noun needs *a/an* the first time and *the* once the listener knows which one.

entries.term: a / an with jobs: She's an engineer
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: After *be*, *work as* or *become*, a singular job or role needs *a/an*: *She's an engineer*, *He works as a nurse*.
entries.usage: Required in all registers; leaving it out is a very noticeable error for speakers of German, French, Spanish, Russian and many other languages. There is no article with plural jobs (*They're nurses*) or with a unique position (*She became CEO in 2019*, *He was elected mayor*).
entries.pattern: be / work as / become + a / an + singular job
examples: My brother's **a firefighter** in Cleveland, so he works crazy hours.
She worked **as a waitress** to pay her way through college.
My daughter wants to be **an astronaut** when she grows up.

drill.sentence: My sister is {{an}} electrician, so she rewired our whole house for free.
drill.hint: Add the missing word: My sister is electrician, so she rewired our whole house for free.

mistake.wrong: I'm student at Ohio State.
mistake.right: I'm a student at Ohio State.
mistake.why: A singular job or role after *be* needs *a/an*.

entries.term: how much vs. how many: how much time / how many people
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *How much* asks about an amount of something uncountable (*time, money, water*); *how many* asks about a number of countable things (*people, days, emails*).
entries.usage: Basic and neutral. *How much* alone also asks about price (*How much is it?*). Watch nouns that are uncountable in English but countable in other languages, such as *information, advice, luggage, furniture* and *homework*.
entries.pattern: how much + uncountable noun / how many + plural noun
examples: **How many people** are coming to the barbecue on Saturday?
**How much time** do we have before the movie starts?
**How much homework** did the kids get tonight?

drill.sentence: {{How much}} furniture are you taking to the new apartment?
drill.hint: Choose how much or how many: ___ furniture are you taking to the new apartment?

mistake.wrong: How many informations do you need from me?
mistake.right: How much information do you need from me?
mistake.why: *Information* is uncountable in English (unlike German *Informationen*), so it takes *how much* and has no plural.

entries.term: a lot vs. a lot of: I like it a lot / a lot of people
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *A lot of* comes before a noun (*a lot of people*); *a lot* without *of* stands alone or comes after a verb (*I like it a lot*).
entries.usage: Both are very common in speech and informal writing; in formal writing, *many, much* or *a great deal of* sound better. *Lots of* is a more casual variant. The verb agrees with the noun after *of*: *A lot of people are …*, *A lot of money is …*.
entries.pattern: a lot of + noun / verb + a lot
examples: There were **a lot of** families at the beach today.
I miss my friends back home **a lot**, especially around the holidays.
We've been eating out **a lot** lately.

drill.sentence: My kids play {{a lot of}} video games on the weekends.
drill.hint: Complete with a lot or a lot of: My kids play ___ video games on the weekends.

mistake.wrong: We have a lot work to do before Friday.
mistake.right: We have a lot of work to do before Friday.
mistake.why: Before a noun, *a lot* needs *of*.

entries.term: some in offers and requests: Would you like some coffee?
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In questions that are offers or requests, *some* is normal because you expect or hope for a *yes*: *Would you like some coffee?*, *Can I have some water?*
entries.usage: *Some* in a question signals that you expect or want a *yes*, so offers sound warm and requests sound natural. *Any* belongs in open questions (*Do you have any questions?*); in a request (*Can I have any water?*), it sounds as if you doubt there is any. *Something* works the same way, though *anything* is also common in offers (*Can I get you anything?*).
entries.pattern: Would you like / Can I have / Could I get + some (+ noun)?
examples: Would you like **some** more pie? There's plenty left.
Can I borrow **some** sugar? I ran out halfway through the recipe.
Can I get you **something** to drink while you wait?

drill.sentence: Could I have {{some}} water, please? I'm really thirsty.
drill.hint: Choose some or any: Could I have ___ water, please? I'm really thirsty.

mistake.wrong: Excuse me, could we have any more napkins?
mistake.right: Excuse me, could we have some more napkins?
mistake.why: In a request, you want a *yes*, so use *some*; *any* sounds as if you doubt there are any left.

entries.term: any in questions and negatives: Do you have any questions?
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Any* is used in open questions and after a negative verb, with plural or uncountable nouns: *Do you have any questions?*, *We don't have any bread*.
entries.usage: Very common in all registers. In questions, *any* is neutral and open (you don't know the answer); *some* would suggest you expect a *yes*. *Any* also follows words with a negative meaning, such as *never, hardly* and *without* (*She left without any money*).
entries.pattern: Do you have any …? / not + any + plural or uncountable noun
examples: Do you have **any** allergies we should know about?
There aren't **any** good restaurants near our hotel.
Did you get **any** sleep on the flight?

drill.sentence: There {{isn't any}} milk left in the fridge.
drill.hint: Make it negative with any: There's some milk left in the fridge.

mistake.wrong: I don't have some cash on me right now.
mistake.right: I don't have any cash on me right now.
mistake.why: After a negative verb, use *any*, not *some*.

entries.term: no double negative: I didn't see anyone
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Standard English uses only one negative word per clause: *I didn't see anyone* or *I saw no one*, not *I didn't see nobody*.
entries.usage: Double negatives are normal in several American dialects and in song lyrics, but standard speech and writing treat them as errors. After *not / n't*, use *any-* words (*anything, anyone, anywhere, ever*); without *not*, use *no-* words. Speakers of Spanish, French, Italian, Russian and other languages that require two negatives often make this error.
entries.pattern: not + any- word / no- word with a positive verb
examples: I **couldn't find my keys anywhere**, so I was late for work.
**Don't tell anyone**, but I'm thinking of quitting.
**Nobody** knows where the cat goes at night.

drill.sentence: I was home all day, but I didn't hear {{anything}}.
drill.hint: Correct the double negative, keeping didn't: I was home all day, but I didn't hear nothing.

mistake.wrong: We didn't go nowhere last summer.
mistake.right: We didn't go anywhere last summer.
mistake.why: After *didn't*, use an *any-* word; a second negative word makes the sentence nonstandard.

entries.term: another vs. other vs. the others: another coffee / other people / the others
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Another* (one more, or a different one) goes with a singular noun; *other* goes with plural nouns; *the others* means the rest of a known group.
entries.usage: *Another* is one word (*an* + *other*), so it never follows *the* or *a*. *Others* with *-s* is a pronoun used without a noun (*Some liked it; others didn't*); before a noun, *other* never takes *-s*. *The other* + singular means the second of two (*the other shoe*).
entries.pattern: another + singular noun / other + plural noun / the others (= the rest)
examples: Can we get **another** bottle of water for the table?
Some people love the heat; **other** people can't stand it.
Lena's already here, but **the others** are stuck in traffic.

drill.sentence: There were eight of us. Three took the train, and {{the others}} drove up on Saturday.
drill.hint: Choose another, other, others or the others: There were eight of us. Three took the train, and ___ drove up on Saturday.

mistake.wrong: We visited Rome and two others cities.
mistake.right: We visited Rome and two other cities.
mistake.why: Before a noun, *other* never takes *-s*; *others* is used only alone, as a pronoun.

entries.term: must vs. have to: I must go / I have to go
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Must* expresses an obligation that the speaker feels or imposes; *have to* expresses an obligation from outside, such as rules or schedules. In everyday American speech, *have to* is used for both.
entries.usage: In American conversation, *must* for obligation sounds strong or formal; it is mostly found in written rules and instructions (*All visitors must sign in*). Americans say *I have to go* or *I've got to go* rather than *I must go*. *Must* has no past or future form, so use *had to* or *will have to*.
entries.pattern: must + base verb (written rules, strong) / have to + base verb (everyday)
examples: Sorry, I **have to** leave early to pick up my son.
All passengers **must** wear a seat belt while the sign is on.
You **have to** try the tacos at this place; they're amazing.

drill.sentence: My bus leaves in five minutes, so I really {{have to}} go.
drill.hint: Say it the everyday American way, with have: My bus leaves in five minutes, so I really must go.

mistake.wrong: Do you must work this Saturday?
mistake.right: Do you have to work this Saturday?
mistake.why: *Must* does not form questions with *do*; in everyday English, ask *Do you have to …?*

entries.term: don't have to vs. mustn't: You don't have to come / You mustn't tell anyone
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Don't have to* means something is not necessary (you can if you want); *mustn't* means it is not allowed or is a bad idea.
entries.usage: Mixing them up changes the message completely. *Don't have to* is very common in all registers. *Mustn't* is rare in American English and sounds British or very formal; Americans say *can't*, *shouldn't* or *aren't allowed to*, and written rules use *must not*.
entries.pattern: don't / doesn't have to + verb (not necessary) / mustn't, can't + verb (not allowed)
examples: It's a casual party, so you **don't have to** wear a tie.
We **don't have to** be at the airport until ten.
Patients **must not** eat or drink anything after midnight before surgery.

drill.sentence: Tomorrow's a holiday, so I {{don't have to}} get up early.
drill.hint: Choose mustn't or don't have to: Tomorrow's a holiday, so I ___ get up early.

mistake.wrong: You mustn't come to the party if you're busy.
mistake.right: You don't have to come to the party if you're busy.
mistake.why: *Mustn't* means it is forbidden; German *musst nicht* (= not necessary) is *don't have to* in English.

entries.term: had to for past obligation: I had to work late
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Had to* + verb expresses obligation or necessity in the past: *I had to work late* means it was necessary for me to work late.
entries.usage: *Must* has no past form, so *had to* covers all past obligation. Questions and negatives use *did*: *Did you have to wait?*, *We didn't have to pay*. Do not confuse it with *must have* + past participle, which is a guess about the past (*She must have left*).
entries.pattern: had to + base verb / did … have to? / didn't have to
examples: I **had to** work late, so I missed my daughter's school play.
**Did** you **have to** wait long at the DMV?
The flight was overbooked, so two passengers **had to** take a later one.

drill.sentence: My car was in the shop last week, so I {{had to}} take the bus every day.
drill.hint: Express the past obligation: My car was in the shop last week, so I must take the bus every day.

mistake.wrong: Yesterday I must work until nine.
mistake.right: Yesterday I had to work until nine.
mistake.why: *Must* has no past form; for a past obligation, use *had to*.

entries.term: should for advice: You should see a doctor
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Should* + base verb gives advice or says what is the right or sensible thing to do: *You should see a doctor*.
entries.usage: The normal way to give advice in every register; *I think you should* or *Maybe you should* makes it softer. *Ought to* means the same but is less common in American speech and sounds a little more formal. *Had better* is stronger and suggests a bad result if you don't.
entries.pattern: should / shouldn't + base verb
examples: That cough sounds bad. You **should** get it checked out.
It's starting to snow. We **should** probably head home soon.
You really **shouldn't** text while you're driving.

drill.sentence: If your back still hurts tomorrow, {{you should}} see a physical therapist.
drill.hint: Give advice with the most common modal (not ought to): If your back still hurts tomorrow, it's a good idea to see a physical therapist.

mistake.wrong: You should to drink more water in this heat.
mistake.right: You should drink more water in this heat.
mistake.why: *Should* is a modal verb, so the base form follows without *to*.

entries.term: must be for present deduction: She must be tired
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Must be* (or *must* + verb) expresses a confident conclusion from evidence: *She must be tired* means I'm almost sure she's tired because of what I see or know.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, often as a sympathetic reaction (*You must be exhausted!*, *That must be hard*). It is a conclusion, not something you know for a fact. The opposite is *can't be*; for a weaker guess, use *might be*.
entries.pattern: must be + adjective / noun; must + base verb
examples: You've been traveling all day. You **must be** starving.
Their lights have been off all week. They **must be** away on vacation.
She **must** really **love** that band; she's seen them five times this year.

drill.sentence: You ran a marathon this morning? You {{must be}} exhausted!
drill.hint: Say you're almost sure: You ran a marathon this morning? I'm sure you're exhausted!

mistake.wrong: Someone's at the door. It can be the pizza guy.
mistake.right: Someone's at the door. It must be the pizza guy.
mistake.why: For a confident guess about now, use *must be* (or *might be* if you are unsure); *can be* means *is sometimes*.

entries.term: can't be for present deduction: That can't be right
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Can't be* expresses a confident negative conclusion, when you are sure something is not true or not possible: *That can't be right*.
entries.usage: Very common in speech, often as a reaction to surprising news or numbers (*That can't be right!*, *You can't be hungry already!*). It is the negative partner of *must be*. Americans also use *must not* here (*They must not know yet*), which sounds a little less certain than *can't*.
entries.pattern: can't be + adjective / noun / -ing; can't + base verb
examples: Forty dollars for a burger? That **can't be** right.
She **can't be** home yet; she only left the office ten minutes ago.
You **can't be** serious! You're quitting tomorrow?

drill.sentence: He {{can't be}} the new manager; he looks about nineteen!
drill.hint: Choose must be or can't be: He ___ the new manager; he looks about nineteen!

mistake.wrong: "Was that Jen at the concert last night?" "It can't be Jen; she was in Denver all weekend."
mistake.right: "Was that Jen at the concert last night?" "It can't have been Jen; she was in Denver all weekend."
mistake.why: *Can't be* is for a conclusion about the present; for the past, use *can't have been* (or *couldn't have been*).

entries.term: might / may / could be: He might be in a meeting
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Might be*, *may be* and *could be* say that something is possibly true now, without certainty: *He might be in a meeting* means perhaps he is.
entries.usage: *Might* is the most frequent in American speech, *may* sounds a bit more formal, and *could* is common when you suggest an explanation (*It could be the battery*). *Might not* and *may not* mean *perhaps not*, but *couldn't be* means *it's impossible*, like *can't be*.
entries.pattern: might / may / could + be (+ adjective / noun / -ing)
examples: Try her cell; she **might be** on her way home.
The car won't start. It **could be** the battery.
Don't worry if he doesn't answer. He **may be** with a patient.

drill.sentence: I haven't seen Ben all day. He {{might be}} at the gym, but I'm not sure.
drill.hint: Choose must be or might be: I haven't seen Ben all day. He ___ at the gym, but I'm not sure.

mistake.wrong: May be she's stuck in traffic.
mistake.right: Maybe she's stuck in traffic.
mistake.why: *Maybe* (one word) is an adverb meaning *perhaps*; *may be* (two words) is a verb: *She may be stuck in traffic*.

entries.term: Can I / Could I / May I for permission: Could I borrow your pen?
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: All three ask for permission: *Can I* is casual and direct, *Could I* is more polite, and *May I* is formal and very polite.
entries.usage: *Can I* is fine with friends and family and in most stores; *Could I* is a safe choice with strangers and at work. *May I* is common in service settings (*May I help you?*) and when you want to show respect. To give permission, say *Sure* or *Yes, you can*, not *Yes, you could*.
entries.pattern: Can / Could / May + I + base verb …?
examples: **Could I** borrow your car on Saturday? Mine's in the shop.
**Can I** have a bite of your sandwich?
Good afternoon, Dr. Kim's office. **May I** ask what this is regarding?

drill.sentence: Excuse me, {{could I}} sit here, or is this seat taken?
drill.hint: Make it more polite, but not formal (not may): Excuse me, can I sit here, or is this seat taken?

mistake.wrong: "Could I use your phone?" "Yes, you could."
mistake.right: "Could I use your phone?" "Sure, go ahead."
mistake.why: *Could* in the question only adds politeness; to give permission, answer with *can* or a phrase like *Sure*.

entries.term: Could you / Would you for requests: Could you send me the file?
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Could you* and *Would you* + base verb make polite requests; *Can you* is more casual and direct.
entries.usage: *Could you* is the safest neutral choice in emails and at work. *Would you* is also polite, but with an impatient tone it can sound like an order (*Would you please stop that?*). For an even softer request, use *Would you mind* + *-ing*.
entries.pattern: Could / Would / Can you + base verb …? / Would you mind + -ing?
examples: **Could you** send me the address when you get a chance?
**Would you** hold the door for me, please?
**Can you** turn the TV down a little? I'm on the phone.

drill.sentence: {{Could you}} save me a seat if you get there first?
drill.hint: Make the request more polite (not would): Can you save me a seat if you get there first?

mistake.wrong: Would you mind to send me the file again?
mistake.right: Would you mind sending me the file again?
mistake.why: *Would you mind* is followed by *-ing*, not *to* + verb.

entries.term: much / far / a lot + comparative: much better, far more expensive
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Much, far, a lot* and, informally, *way* before a comparative say that the difference is big: *much better*, *far more expensive*.
entries.usage: *Much* is neutral, *far* is a bit more emphatic or formal, and *a lot* and *way* are casual (*way better*). *Very* cannot modify a comparative (*very better* is wrong). Before *more* + plural noun, use *many more* (*many more people*).
entries.pattern: much / far / a lot / way + comparative
examples: Our new apartment is **much bigger** than the old one.
Flying is **far more expensive** than driving at this time of year.
I feel **a lot better** since I started walking to work.

drill.sentence: This mattress is {{much}} more comfortable than our old one.
drill.hint: Correct the intensifier, using the neutral word: This mattress is very more comfortable than our old one.

mistake.wrong: There were much more people at the game than last year.
mistake.right: There were many more people at the game than last year.
mistake.why: Before *more* + a plural noun, use *many more*, not *much more*.

entries.term: a bit / slightly + comparative: a bit cheaper, slightly higher
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *A bit, a little* and *slightly* before a comparative show that the difference is small: *a bit cheaper*, *slightly higher*.
entries.usage: *A bit* and *a little* are common in conversation; *slightly* is neutral to formal and common in reports and news (*slightly higher than expected*). In requests, they make you sound polite: *Could you speak a bit more slowly?*
entries.pattern: a bit / a little / slightly + comparative
examples: Can we sit **a bit closer** to the front? I can't see the screen.
The blue one is **slightly cheaper**, but I like the green one better.
Unemployment was **slightly lower** last month than economists expected.

drill.sentence: Gas prices were {{slightly}} higher in July than in June.
drill.hint: Rewrite in news style, replacing a bit (one word, not marginally or somewhat): Gas prices were a bit higher in July than in June.

mistake.wrong: This hotel is a few cheaper than the other one.
mistake.right: This hotel is a little cheaper than the other one.
mistake.why: *A few* goes with plural nouns; before a comparative, use *a little*, *a bit* or *slightly*.

entries.term: as … as: as fast as / just as good as
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *As* + adjective or adverb + *as* says that two things are equal in some quality: *She's as tall as her mother*.
entries.usage: Neutral and very common. The second word is *as*, not *than* or *like*. *Just as* stresses that they are really equal, while *almost as* or *nearly as* says that one is a little less.
entries.pattern: (just / almost / nearly) as + adjective / adverb + as
examples: The sequel is **just as good as** the first movie.
My fourteen-year-old son is already **as tall as** his dad.
I'll get there **as fast as** I can, I promise.

drill.sentence: The homemade bread is {{as good as}} the bread from the bakery.
drill.hint: Rewrite with as … as: The homemade bread and the bread from the bakery are equally good.

mistake.wrong: My phone is as old than yours.
mistake.right: My phone is as old as yours.
mistake.why: An equal comparison is *as … as*; *than* follows only a comparative (*older than*).

entries.term: not as … as: It's not as hard as I thought
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Not as* + adjective or adverb + *as* says that the first thing has less of a quality than the second: *It's not as hard as I thought* means it's easier than I thought.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, where it sounds more natural than *less … than* (*less hard than* sounds odd). It is also a polite way to criticize (*The service isn't as good as it used to be*). *Not so … as* means the same but sounds formal or dated in American English.
entries.pattern: not as + adjective / adverb + as
examples: The hike **wasn't as hard as** everyone said, even with the steep part at the end.
Their new album **isn't as good as** the last one.
I **don't run as fast as** I used to, but I still run every morning.

drill.sentence: This summer {{wasn't as hot as}} last summer.
drill.hint: Rewrite with not as … as: Last summer was hotter than this summer.

mistake.wrong: The movie was less good than the book.
mistake.right: The movie wasn't as good as the book.
mistake.why: *Less* sounds unnatural with short adjectives like *good, big* or *hard*; use *not as … as*.

entries.term: superlative + ever with present perfect: the best movie I've ever seen
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A superlative + a clause with *ever* describes the most extreme case in someone's experience up to now: *the best movie I've ever seen*.
entries.usage: Very common in speech, reviews and social media, usually with the present perfect (*I've ever had*). In American speech, the simple past is also common (*the best teacher I ever had*), especially for a finished period. Use *ever*, not *never*, after the superlative.
entries.pattern: the + superlative + noun + (that) + subject + have ever + past participle
examples: Honestly, that's **the best pizza I've ever had**.
This is **the hardest decision I've ever had to make**.
She's **the funniest person I've ever met**, and she doesn't even try.

drill.sentence: This is {{the most beautiful beach I've ever seen}}.
drill.hint: Rewrite with a superlative + ever: I've never seen such a beautiful beach.

mistake.wrong: It's the best movie I have never seen.
mistake.right: It's the best movie I have ever seen.
mistake.why: After a superlative, use *ever*; *never* would mean you haven't seen it.

entries.term: no double comparative: cheaper, not 'more cheaper'
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A comparative uses either *-er* (short adjectives) or *more* (longer ones), never both: *cheaper* and *more expensive*, not *more cheaper*.
entries.usage: One-syllable adjectives take *-er* (*bigger*), and two-syllable adjectives ending in *-y* take *-ier* (*easier*). Most other adjectives of two or more syllables take *more* (*more careful*, *more modern*), though a few allow both (*quieter*, *more quiet*). Irregular forms such as *better, worse* and *farther* never take *more*.
entries.pattern: short adjective + -er / more + longer adjective (never both)
examples: Let's take the train; it's **cheaper** and usually **faster**.
The second interview was **more relaxed** than the first one.
My cold is **worse** today than it was yesterday.

drill.sentence: This route is {{shorter}} than the one the GPS suggested.
drill.hint: Correct the comparative: This route is more shorter than the one the GPS suggested.

mistake.wrong: This phone is more better than my old one.
mistake.right: This phone is much better than my old one.
mistake.why: *Better* is already a comparative; to make it stronger, use *much* or *a lot*, not *more*.

entries.term: one of the + superlative + plural: one of the best restaurants
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *One of the* + superlative + plural noun picks out one member of a top group: *one of the best restaurants in town*.
entries.usage: Very common in speech, reviews and writing, often as a softer claim than a plain superlative. The noun is always plural. When *one* is the subject, the verb is singular: *One of the best players is injured*.
entries.pattern: one of the + superlative + plural noun (+ singular verb)
examples: Yellowstone is **one of the most popular parks** in the country.
That was **one of the hardest years** of my life.
**One of the biggest problems** in our building is the noise from the bar downstairs.

drill.sentence: Lisbon is one of the most beautiful {{cities}} I've ever visited.
drill.hint: Correct the noun: Lisbon is one of the most beautiful city I've ever visited.

mistake.wrong: He's one of best players on the team.
mistake.right: He's one of the best players on the team.
mistake.why: A superlative needs *the*, so the pattern is *one of the* + superlative + plural noun.

entries.term: question tags: It's late, isn't it?
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: A short question at the end of a statement (*isn't it?*, *do you?*) asks the listener to confirm or agree; a positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement a positive tag.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation. The tag repeats the auxiliary or *be* from the statement (*You've met her, haven't you?*), or uses *do / does / did* if there is none (*She lives here, doesn't she?*). In casual American speech, *right?* is a very common tag that never changes.
entries.pattern: positive statement, negative auxiliary + pronoun? / negative statement, positive auxiliary + pronoun?
examples: It's freezing out there today, **isn't it**?
You haven't seen my keys anywhere, **have you**?
She works at the children's hospital, **doesn't she**?

drill.sentence: You didn't forget the tickets, {{did you}}?
drill.hint: Add a question tag: You didn't forget the tickets.

mistake.wrong: He lives in Austin, isn't it?
mistake.right: He lives in Austin, doesn't he?
mistake.why: The tag repeats the auxiliary and the subject of the statement; *isn't it* is not a general-purpose tag.

entries.term: indirect questions: Could you tell me where the station is?
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: After openings like *Could you tell me* or *Do you know*, a wh-question uses statement word order and no *do*: *Could you tell me where the station is?*
entries.usage: Indirect questions sound more polite than direct ones and are very common with strangers, in stores and in emails. After *I wonder* or *I'd like to know*, the sentence is a statement and ends with a period. The same word order applies after *I don't know* and *I'm not sure*.
entries.pattern: Could you tell me / Do you know + wh-word + subject + verb
examples: Do you know **what time the game starts**?
Could you tell me **where I can find** the restrooms?
I'm not sure **how much the tickets cost**.

drill.sentence: Excuse me, do you know {{where the nearest gas station is}}?
drill.hint: Make it polite: Excuse me, where is the nearest gas station?

mistake.wrong: Can you tell me where is the post office?
mistake.right: Can you tell me where the post office is?
mistake.why: In an indirect question, the subject comes before the verb, as in a statement.

entries.term: indirect yes/no questions: Do you know if she's here?
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: An indirect yes/no question uses *if* or *whether* + statement word order: *Do you know if she's here?* asks *Is she here?* politely.
entries.usage: Very common in polite requests and emails (*I was wondering if …*). *If* is more common in speech; *whether* is more formal. Do not leave out *if / whether* and do not use *do*: *Do you know is she here?* is wrong.
entries.pattern: Do you know / Can you tell me / I wonder + if / whether + subject + verb
examples: Do you know **if the bank is open** on Saturdays?
Can you check **whether my package has arrived**?
I'll text them and ask **if they need a ride** from the airport.

drill.sentence: Could you ask the waiter {{if the soup is}} vegetarian?
drill.hint: Make the question indirect, with if: Could you ask the waiter: is the soup vegetarian?

mistake.wrong: Do you know does this bus go downtown?
mistake.right: Do you know if this bus goes downtown?
mistake.why: An indirect yes/no question needs *if* or *whether* and statement word order, without *do*.

entries.term: subject vs. object questions: Who called you? / Who did you call?
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: When *who* or *what* is the subject, the question uses statement word order and no *do*: *Who called you?* When it is the object, use *do / does / did*: *Who did you call?*
entries.usage: The two forms ask different things: *Who called you?* asks for the caller; *Who did you call?* asks for the person you called. The same applies to *which* + noun and *how many* + noun (*How many people came?*).
entries.pattern: Who / What + verb …? (subject) / Who / What + do / does / did + subject + verb? (object)
examples: **Who told** you about the surprise party? It was supposed to be a secret.
**What happened** to your arm? Did you fall off your bike?
So **who did** you **invite** to the wedding in the end?

drill.sentence: {{Who won}} the game last night?
drill.hint: Ask about the person: Somebody won the game last night.

mistake.wrong: What did happen at the meeting yesterday?
mistake.right: What happened at the meeting yesterday?
mistake.why: *What* is the subject, so the question takes no *did*.

entries.term: might / may for future possibility: I might come later
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Might* or *may* + base verb says that something is possible in the future but not certain: *I might come later* means perhaps I will come.
entries.usage: *Might* is the usual choice in American conversation; *may* is more common in writing, news and announcements (*Delays may occur*). *Might not* and *may not* mean *perhaps not*, but *may not* can also mean *not allowed* in formal rules.
entries.pattern: might / may (not) + base verb
examples: I **might** stop by after work, but don't wait for me.
Bring a jacket; it **might** get cold after sunset.
Some flights **may** be delayed because of the storm.

drill.sentence: I'm not feeling great, so I {{might not}} make it to the party tonight.
drill.hint: Rewrite with might: I'm not feeling great, so perhaps I won't make it to the party tonight.

mistake.wrong: Take an umbrella; it might be rain later.
mistake.right: Take an umbrella; it might rain later.
mistake.why: *Rain* is the verb here, so it follows *might* directly, without *be*.

entries.term: the for things both speakers know: Can you close the door?
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Use *the* when the listener knows which thing you mean because it is the only one in the situation (*the door*, *the kitchen*) or the only one in general (*the sun*).
entries.usage: This works even at first mention: *Can you close the door?* is fine because there is only one door in the room. Shared knowledge in a home, an office or a town works the same way (*the bank*, *the boss*, *the store*).
entries.pattern: the + noun (the listener can tell which one from the situation)
examples: Can you turn off **the lights** when you leave?
I'm running to **the store**. Need anything?
**The sun** is really strong today, so don't forget sunscreen.

drill.sentence: Could you take {{the}} trash out before you go to bed?
drill.hint: Add the missing article: Could you take trash out before you go to bed?

mistake.wrong: I'm going to supermarket. Do you need anything?
mistake.right: I'm going to the supermarket. Do you need anything?
mistake.why: The listener knows which supermarket you mean (your usual one), so use *the*.

entries.term: no article with meals, sports and languages: have lunch, play tennis
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Meals (*breakfast, lunch, dinner*), sports and games (*tennis, chess*) and languages (*German, Spanish*) take no article when used in general.
entries.usage: Use an article only when the noun is specific or described: *a big breakfast*, *the dinner we had in Rome*. A language name on its own takes no article; with some nationality words, *the* means the people (*the Spanish*, *the French*).
entries.pattern: have + breakfast / lunch / dinner; play + sport; speak / learn + language (no article)
examples: Do you want to get **lunch** on Friday?
My kids play **soccer** every Saturday morning.
She grew up speaking **Korean** at home and **English** at school.

drill.sentence: We usually have {{dinner}} around seven, after the kids' practice.
drill.hint: Correct the sentence: We usually have the dinner around seven, after the kids' practice.

mistake.wrong: I'm learning the Spanish for my new job.
mistake.right: I'm learning Spanish for my new job.
mistake.why: Language names take no article; *the Spanish* means the people of Spain.

entries.term: a / an for rates and frequency: twice a week, $20 an hour
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *A/an* after a number or frequency word means *per* or *each*: *twice a week*, *$20 an hour*, *sixty miles an hour*.
entries.usage: Normal in all everyday contexts; *per* is more formal and common in written prices and rules (*$5 per person*). Use *an* before a vowel sound: *an hour*, but *a year*.
entries.pattern: number / frequency + a / an + time or unit
examples: I try to go to the gym **three times a week**.
The babysitter charges **eighteen dollars an hour**.
The speed limit on this road is **forty-five miles an hour**.

drill.sentence: We eat out about twice {{a}} month.
drill.hint: Replace per with the everyday word: We eat out about twice per month.

mistake.wrong: Take this pill twice in a day.
mistake.right: Take this pill twice a day.
mistake.why: For frequency, *a* already means *per*, so no *in* is needed.

entries.term: no article before next / last + time: next week, last year
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: With *next, last, this* and *every* + a time word, English uses no article and no preposition: *next week*, *last year*, *this Friday*.
entries.usage: Do not add *on, in* or *the*: *on next Monday* and *in last year* are wrong. *The next week* and *the last week* mean something different: a seven-day period after another point, or the seven days up to now (*I've been sick for the last week*).
entries.pattern: next / last / this / every + time word (no article, no preposition)
examples: We're moving to Portland **next month**, so we're packing every night.
I ran into them at the hardware store **last Saturday**.
**This year** we're spending Thanksgiving at my sister's place.

drill.sentence: The dentist can see you {{next Tuesday}} at ten.
drill.hint: Correct the time phrase: The dentist can see you on the next Tuesday at ten.

mistake.wrong: I started this job in last March.
mistake.right: I started this job last March.
mistake.why: *Last, next* and *this* + a time word take no preposition.

entries.term: plenty of: We have plenty of time
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Plenty of* + noun means *a lot, more than enough*: *We have plenty of time*.
entries.usage: Neutral and friendly, often used to reassure people (*Don't worry, there's plenty of food*). It goes with plural and uncountable nouns and is mainly used in positive sentences and questions; in negatives, use *not much* or *not enough*. *Plenty* can also stand alone (*No thanks, I've got plenty*).
entries.pattern: plenty of + plural / uncountable noun
examples: There's **plenty of parking** behind the building.
Make sure the kids drink **plenty of water** in this heat.
We have **plenty of extra blankets** if you get cold tonight.

drill.sentence: Don't buy more chips; we already have {{plenty of}} snacks for the party.
drill.hint: Rewrite with plenty: Don't buy more chips; we already have more than enough snacks for the party.

mistake.wrong: Relax, we have plenty time before the train leaves.
mistake.right: Relax, we have plenty of time before the train leaves.
mistake.why: Before a noun, *plenty* needs *of*.

entries.term: no + noun vs. not any: There's no milk / There isn't any milk
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *There's no coffee* and *There isn't any coffee* mean the same; *no* + noun sounds a little stronger or more definite.
entries.usage: Use *no* with a positive verb and *any* with a negative verb, never both in one clause. *No* sounds more definite and is typical of signs and rules (*No parking*); with a singular countable noun, *no* is often the natural choice (*There's no reason to worry*). In conversation, *isn't any* is a little softer and very common.
entries.pattern: positive verb + no + noun / negative verb + any + noun
examples: Sorry, there's **no** hot water this morning; the water heater is broken.
We have **no** plans for the weekend yet.
**No** dogs are allowed on the beach in summer.

drill.sentence: We {{have no}} idea what to get her for her birthday.
drill.hint: Rewrite with no: We don't have any idea what to get her for her birthday.

mistake.wrong: There's not parking anywhere near the stadium.
mistake.right: There's no parking anywhere near the stadium.
mistake.why: Before a noun, use *no* (or *isn't any*); *not* goes with a verb.

entries.term: each vs. every: each of us / every day
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Each* looks at the members of a group one by one and can be used for two; *every* looks at all the members of a group of three or more together.
entries.usage: Often both are possible (*each day*, *every day*). Use *each* for two (*each hand*) and *each of* + plural noun or pronoun (*each of us*); *every of* is wrong, but *every one of us* is fine. Use *every* with *almost* or *nearly* and for intervals (*every two weeks*).
entries.pattern: each (of) + noun / every + singular noun / every one of
examples: She came in with a cup of coffee in **each hand**.
We walk the dog **every morning** before work.
**Each of** us paid for our own ticket.

drill.sentence: {{Each of}} my cousins got a different present from Grandma.
drill.hint: Correct the sentence (two words): Every of my cousins got a different present from Grandma.

mistake.wrong: I check my email almost each hour.
mistake.right: I check my email almost every hour.
mistake.why: *Almost* and *nearly* go with *every*, not *each*.

entries.term: too much / too many: too much work / too many emails
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Too much* + uncountable noun and *too many* + plural noun mean more than is good or acceptable: *too much work*, *too many emails*.
entries.usage: Very common for complaints. *Too much* also works alone after a verb (*You worry too much*). Before an adjective, use *too* or *much too*, not *too much* (*too much expensive* is wrong).
entries.pattern: too much + uncountable noun / too many + plural noun / verb + too much
examples: I've had **too much coffee** today; my hands are shaking.
There are **too many tourists** in the old town in August.
You spend **too much time** on your phone.

drill.sentence: I can't go out tonight; I have {{too much}} homework.
drill.hint: Choose too much or too many: I can't go out tonight; I have ___ homework.

mistake.wrong: There's too many traffic downtown at five.
mistake.right: There's too much traffic downtown at five.
mistake.why: *Traffic* is uncountable, so it takes *too much*.

entries.term: don't need to for no necessity: You don't need to bring anything
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Don't need to* + verb means something is not necessary: *You don't need to bring anything*.
entries.usage: It means about the same as *don't have to* and is very common in American English, while *needn't* sounds British or formal to most Americans. *Didn't need to* says that something was not necessary in the past, whether or not it was done.
entries.pattern: don't / doesn't / didn't need to + base verb
examples: You **don't need to** take your shoes off; come on in.
We **didn't need to** book a table; the place was half empty.
You **don't need to** print your ticket; just show it on your phone.

drill.sentence: It's a casual dinner, so you {{don't need to}} dress up.
drill.hint: Rewrite the American way, keeping need: It's a casual dinner, so you needn't dress up.

mistake.wrong: You don't need bring anything to the party.
mistake.right: You don't need to bring anything to the party.
mistake.why: In American English, *need* is a normal verb, so it takes *to* + verb.

entries.term: be supposed to for rules: You're not supposed to park here
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Be supposed to* + verb says what a rule, an agreement or other people expect you to do: *You're not supposed to park here* means it's not allowed.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation; it is softer and less direct than *must* or *can't*. It often suggests that the rule is sometimes broken (*We're supposed to wear helmets, but nobody does*). *Not supposed to* is the usual polite way to say that something isn't allowed.
entries.pattern: be (not) supposed to + base verb
examples: You're **not supposed to** eat in the library.
We're **supposed to** check out of the hotel by eleven.
Am I **supposed to** tip the delivery driver?

drill.sentence: Hurry up! {{We're supposed to}} be there by seven.
drill.hint: Rewrite with supposed to: Hurry up! They expect us to be there by seven.

mistake.wrong: We're suppose to bring our own towels.
mistake.right: We're supposed to bring our own towels.
mistake.why: The *-d* is hard to hear in speech, but it is always written: *supposed to*.

entries.term: can't for rules: You can't park here
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Can't* (or *cannot*) says that something is not allowed by a rule or by the speaker: *You can't park here*.
entries.usage: The normal way to state a prohibition in American speech; *mustn't* sounds British or old-fashioned, and *may not* is formal (*Guests may not bring food into the pool area*). In the same way, *can* gives permission (*You can park on the street after six*).
entries.pattern: can't / cannot + base verb (not allowed)
examples: Sorry, you **can't** bring drinks into the theater.
Since last year, you **can't** smoke anywhere on campus, even outdoors.
Kids under twelve **can't** ride without an adult.

drill.sentence: Sorry, you {{can't}} swim here today; there's no lifeguard on duty.
drill.hint: Say it the everyday American way: Sorry, you mustn't swim here today; there's no lifeguard on duty.

mistake.wrong: It's not allowed to park in front of the garage.
mistake.right: You can't park in front of the garage.
mistake.why: English doesn't use *It's not allowed to* + verb; say *You can't park …*, *You're not allowed to park …* or *Parking isn't allowed …*.

entries.term: be able to in other forms: will be able to, have been able to
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Can* has only two forms, *can* and *could*, so *be able to* fills the other forms: *will be able to*, *have been able to*, *might be able to*, *to be able to*.
entries.usage: Use *will be able to* for a future ability that depends on something new (*Once I get my license, I'll be able to drive*); for plans and arrangements, *can* is fine (*I can come tomorrow*). After another modal or after verbs like *want* and *hope*, only *be able to* works.
entries.pattern: will / might / should be able to; have / has been able to; to be able to + base verb
examples: After the surgery, she **won't be able to** drive for a few weeks.
We **haven't been able to** reach anyone at the insurance company.
With the new scanner, the lab **will be able to** process twice as many samples.

drill.sentence: I {{haven't been able to}} sleep well since we moved.
drill.hint: Correct the verb (present perfect): I can't sleep well since we moved.

mistake.wrong: I will can help you with the move next week.
mistake.right: I'll be able to help you with the move next week.
mistake.why: *Can* cannot follow another modal like *will*; use *be able to*.

entries.term: twice as … as: twice as expensive as
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Twice, three times* or *half* + *as … as* compares two things by a multiple: *twice as expensive as* means two times the price.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and reports. Before a noun, use *as much* or *as many* (*twice as many people*). *Three times bigger than* is also common, but *twice* and *half* normally use *as … as* (*twice bigger* is nonstandard).
entries.pattern: twice / three times / half + as + adjective (or much / many + noun) + as
examples: Rent here is **twice as high as** in my hometown.
Our new fridge uses **half as much electricity as** the old one.
There were **three times as many people as** last year, so we ran out of food.

drill.sentence: The new bridge is {{twice as long as}} the old one.
drill.hint: Rewrite with twice as … as: The new bridge is double the length of the old one.

mistake.wrong: This phone is twice more expensive than mine.
mistake.right: This phone is twice as expensive as mine.
mistake.why: With *twice* and *half*, use *as … as*, not a comparative with *than*.

entries.term: comparative and comparative: better and better, more and more
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Repeating a comparative (*better and better*, *more and more expensive*) shows a change that keeps going.
entries.usage: Common in speech and storytelling, often with *get* or *become* (*It's getting harder and harder*). With long adjectives, repeat only *more*: *more and more difficult*. *Less and less* shows a steady decrease.
entries.pattern: comparative + and + comparative / more and more + adjective or noun
examples: Her piano playing is getting **better and better**.
Rents in this city are getting **more and more expensive**.
**More and more** people are choosing to bike to work.

drill.sentence: As the night went on, the music got {{louder and louder}}.
drill.hint: Show that the change continued: As the night went on, the music kept getting louder.

mistake.wrong: It's getting more difficult and more difficult to find parking.
mistake.right: It's getting more and more difficult to find parking.
mistake.why: With long adjectives, repeat only *more* and say the adjective once.

entries.term: different from / different than (US): It's different than I expected
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: Both introduce the thing being compared after *different*; *different than* is normal in American English, especially before a clause (*different than I expected*).
entries.usage: *Different from* is accepted everywhere and is the safest choice in formal writing. *Different than* is standard in American speech and in much American writing, and it is smoother before a clause (*different than it used to be*, instead of *different from what it used to be*). *Different to* is British.
entries.pattern: different from + noun / different than + noun or clause (US)
examples: The neighborhood looks **different than** I remember it.
Her accent is a little **different from** her brother's.
Working from home is very **different than** working in an office.

drill.sentence: The new version of the app is totally {{different than}} it used to be.
drill.hint: Shorten it the American way, without what: The new version of the app is totally different from what it used to be.

mistake.wrong: My new job is very different of my old one.
mistake.right: My new job is very different from my old one.
mistake.why: *Different* takes *from* (or *than* in American English), not *of*.

entries.term: much too + adjective: much too expensive
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Much too* (or *far too*, *way too*) + adjective or adverb makes *too* stronger: *much too expensive* means far more than is acceptable.
entries.usage: *Much too* is neutral, *far too* is a bit more formal, and *way too* is very common in casual American speech. The order matters: *too much* goes before a noun (*too much sugar*), *much too* before an adjective (*much too sweet*).
entries.pattern: much / far / way + too + adjective / adverb
examples: That dress is **much too expensive** for something I'll wear once.
It's **way too early** to start decorating for Christmas!
The instructions were **far too complicated** for a simple bookshelf.

drill.sentence: These shoes are {{much too}} small for him now.
drill.hint: Correct the word order: These shoes are too much small for him now.

mistake.wrong: It's very too hot to sit outside today.
mistake.right: It's much too hot to sit outside today.
mistake.why: *Very* cannot make *too* stronger; use *much, far* or *way*.

entries.term: question tag after I'm: I'm late, aren't I?
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: The negative tag after *I am* is *aren't I*: *I'm late, aren't I?* Forms like *am not I* are wrong, and *amn't I* is not standard American English.
entries.usage: Natural in all registers, even though *I aren't* is impossible as a statement. *Am I not* is possible but sounds very formal. After a negative statement, the tag is regular: *I'm not late, am I?*
entries.pattern: I'm + …, aren't I? / I'm not + …, am I?
examples: I'm next in line, **aren't I**?
I'm invited to the barbecue too, **aren't I**?
I'm not in your way here, **am I**?

drill.sentence: I'm right about this, {{aren't I}}?
drill.hint: Add a question tag: I'm right about this.

mistake.wrong: I'm older than you, am not I?
mistake.right: I'm older than you, aren't I?
mistake.why: The negative tag for *I am* is irregular: *aren't I*.

entries.term: answering negative questions: You're not coming? No, I'm not.
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: In English, *yes* and *no* follow the facts, not the form of the question: *You're not coming? – No, I'm not* (= I'm not coming); *Yes, I am* (= I am coming).
entries.usage: Japanese and Korean speakers often answer the form of the question (*Yes* = right, I'm not coming), and German and French have a special word (*doch*, *si*) to contradict a negative question. In English, use *No* + a negative or *Yes* + a positive, and add the short verb to be clear (*Yes, I am*, *No, I'm not*).
entries.pattern: Negative question? – No + negative (agree) / Yes + positive (contradict)
examples: "You didn't lock the door?" "**No, I didn't**. Sorry!"
"Aren't you hungry?" "**Yes, I'm starving**. Let's eat."
"Don't you like spicy food?" "**No, not really**."

drill.sentence: "You don't eat meat?" "{{No, I don't}}. I've been a vegetarian for years."
drill.hint: Answer, confirming that you don't eat meat: You don't eat meat?

mistake.wrong: "Aren't you tired?" "Yes, I'm not."
mistake.right: "Aren't you tired?" "No, I'm not."
mistake.why: *Yes* goes with a positive answer and *no* with a negative one.

entries.term: position of all and both: We all agreed / They're both busy
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *All* and *both* that refer to the subject go in mid position: before a main verb (*We all agreed*) but after *be* or the first auxiliary (*They're both busy*, *We've all seen it*).
entries.usage: A common, natural alternative to *all of us* or *both of them*. With an object pronoun, they come after it (*I invited them all*, *I love you both*). German puts *alle* after the verb (*Wir stimmten alle zu*), so German speakers often say *We agreed all*.
entries.pattern: subject + all / both + main verb / subject + be or auxiliary + all / both
examples: My parents **both** work night shifts at the hospital.
The kids are **all** asleep, so let's open the wine.
We've **all** been there, so don't feel bad.

drill.sentence: My roommates {{are both}} out of town this weekend.
drill.hint: Put both in the right place: My roommates both are out of town this weekend.

mistake.wrong: We agreed all on the new schedule.
mistake.right: We all agreed on the new schedule.
mistake.why: With a main verb, *all* and *both* go before it.

entries.term: which vs. what in questions: Which one do you want?
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *Which* asks about a choice from a limited, known set (*Which one do you want?*); *what* asks about an open choice (*What do you want for dinner?*).
entries.usage: Both are possible in many cases (*What color* or *Which color do you like?*), but *which* signals that the options are known. Use *which* before *one, ones* and *of* (*which of these*); *what of* is not possible.
entries.pattern: which (one / of) … (limited choice) / what + noun … (open choice)
examples: **Which** of these two photos should I use for my profile?
**What** kind of music do you listen to when you work out?
**Which** gate does our flight leave from, B12 or B14?

drill.sentence: There are two buses at the stop. {{Which}} one goes downtown?
drill.hint: Choose which or what: There are two buses at the stop. ___ one goes downtown?

mistake.wrong: What of these jackets do you like best?
mistake.right: Which of these jackets do you like best?
mistake.why: Before *of*, only *which* is possible.

entries.term: one / ones as a substitute: I'll take the blue one
entries.label: grammar
entries.meaning: *One* (singular) and *ones* (plural) replace a countable noun that was just mentioned, usually after an adjective or *the*: *I'll take the blue one*.
entries.usage: Very common when shopping, choosing and comparing. It replaces only countable nouns (*I prefer red wine to white*, not *white one*). An adjective cannot stand alone in place of the noun: *a new one*, not *a new*.
entries.pattern: a / the / this / which + (adjective) + one / ones
examples: These cookies are good, but the chocolate **ones** are even better.
My phone is really old. I need a new **one**.
"Which car is yours?" "The gray **one** by the gate."

drill.sentence: I don't like the green mugs; let's get the white {{ones}}.
drill.hint: Avoid repeating the noun: I don't like the green mugs; let's get the white mugs.

mistake.wrong: I lost my umbrella, so I bought a new.
mistake.right: I lost my umbrella, so I bought a new one.
mistake.why: An adjective cannot stand alone in place of a countable noun; add *one*.
